cover.artAlt: A bright green tree python coiled in neat loops on a mossy rainforest branch
cover.blurb: Scaly skin, no fur, and a favorite warm rock to sit on. Turn the page and meet the reptiles.

pages.title: Scales, and a Brand New Skin
pages.artAlt: A very close view of a snake's colorful diamond-patterned scales filling the whole picture

facts.text: A snake is covered in scales, and they are dry, not slimy. They are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails. The wide flat scales along a snake's belly work like the treads on a boot and grip the ground.

A snake's skin does not grow with it, so every so often the whole outer layer comes off in one piece. The snake rubs its head on something rough and crawls out, turning the old skin inside out like a sock. A grown-up snake usually does this two to four times a year.
facts.artAlt: A snake crawling forward out of its old skin, the pale empty skin lying behind it turned inside out like a peeled sock
facts.caption: The whole skin peels off in one piece, inside out.

facts.text: No legs, no problem. A single snake can have about 175 to 400 ribs and backbones, joined up by 10,000 to 15,000 tiny muscles. It squeezes those muscles in waves, pushing its curves against the ground to slide forward.
facts.artAlt: A long snake stretched out across warm sand in wide S-shaped curves, its whole body in view from nose to tail tip
facts.caption: Curve after curve pushes on the ground, and the snake slides forward.

infographic.title: How a snake gets a brand new skin

stops.label: About two weeks ahead, the snake stops eating and its skin turns dull
It rubs its head on a rough rock or branch until the old skin splits
It crawls forward and the skin peels off inside out, like pulling off a sock
Out comes a shiny new snake, two to four times a year

infographic.caption: Every step here comes from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. The only number is the two to four sheds a year, which is what a grown-up snake usually manages.

pages.title: The Lizard That Changes Color
pages.artAlt: A chameleon gripping a branch with its tail curled into a spiral and one eye swiveled around backward

facts.text: Chameleons do not change color to match the wallpaper. Each kind has its own set of colors and patterns it can show, and it swaps between them depending on how warm it is, how bright the light is, and how it is feeling. A calm chameleon and a grumpy chameleon are different colors.

Each of a chameleon's eyes turns and focuses on its own. It can watch a beetle on one side and a branch on the other at the very same moment, and between the two eyes it can see nearly all the way around itself.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a chameleon's head, its two cone-shaped eyelids turned so that each eye points a different way
facts.caption: Two eyes, two directions, at the very same moment.

facts.text: The tongue is the surprise. It shoots out in a blink, and in some chameleons it is longer than the whole body. The tip goes sticky and cup shaped so a beetle comes back with it. Meanwhile that curly tail is wrapped tight around the branch like a spare hand.
facts.artAlt: A chameleon with its long tongue shot out straight ahead, the sticky cup-shaped tip touching a cricket on a twig
facts.caption: The tongue fires out, and the beetle comes back with it.

infographic.title: A push harder than a rocket's

rows.label: A fighter jet pulling out of a dive

infographic.caption: All three numbers come from Smithsonian magazine. Gravity's pull is the tug that brings you back down when you jump, and a tongue shoved out 264 times that hard is the strongest push ever measured in a reptile, a bird or a mammal.

pages.title: The Tortoise and Its Shell
pages.artAlt: A giant tortoise walking slowly across sunlit green grass

facts.text: A tortoise cannot climb out of its shell, because the shell is part of its skeleton. It is built from about sixty bones joined to the tortoise's backbone and ribs. So a tortoise wears its ribs on the outside.

The plates on top of the shell are called scutes, and they are made of keratin, just like your fingernails. A tortoise can feel a hand pressing on its shell the way you can feel someone press your nail. Inside, the bone is full of tiny air pockets, which makes the whole shell lighter to carry.
facts.artAlt: A very close view of the top of a tortoise's shell, showing the patterned plates fitted together like tiles with pale lines along every seam
facts.caption: Each patterned plate is a scute, made of the stuff in your fingernails.

facts.text: Giant tortoises are some of the longest lived animals on land. An Aldabra tortoise can pass one hundred years old, and a few have reached over one hundred and fifty. A tortoise plodding across the grass today may have been alive before your great grandparents were born.
facts.artAlt: An old giant tortoise with a worn, weathered dark shell resting on grass, its wrinkled neck stretched right out
facts.caption: This tortoise may be older than anyone you have ever met.

infographic.title: How long can a life be?

rows.label: An Aldabra tortoise
rows.display: more than 100 years, and a few past 150

infographic.caption: The tortoise's great age comes from Smithsonian's National Zoo. The cat and the person are everyday lifetimes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Warming Up in the Sun
pages.artAlt: A small green lizard resting on a warm sunlit rock

facts.text: Reptiles are ectothermic, which means their warmth comes from outside them instead of from inside. You make your own heat all day long. A lizard borrows its heat from the sun, so it lies on a warm rock until it is toasty and ready to move.
That is why a lizard on a rock is not being lazy. It is charging up. Once it is warm it can run, climb and chase insects, and when it gets too hot it slips into the shade to cool down again.
facts.artAlt: A lizard stretched out flat on a sunny rock with its legs splayed wide, soaking up the heat
facts.caption: Flat on a warm rock, charging up for the day.

facts.text: When the weather turns cold, reptiles go slow and quiet, and some settle into a long sleepy rest called brumation until things warm up. Their scaly skin helps too, because it holds water in, which is how so many reptiles do well in dry, sandy places.
facts.artAlt: A lizard tucked into a shady crack between two big rocks, only its head and one front foot showing
facts.caption: Too cold or too hot, and a lizard tucks itself away.

infographic.title: A lizard's sunny day

stops.label: The morning is cool, so the lizard is slow and stays tucked away
It climbs onto a rock in the sun and soaks up the warmth
Now it can run, climb and chase insects
It slips into the shade to cool down again

infographic.caption: Every step comes from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. There are no numbers to count here: a lizard does this all day long, warming up and cooling off.

finish.title: You finished Snakes & Reptiles!
finish.blurb: Next sunny morning, look at the top of a wall or a warm stone and see who is already there soaking up the heat. Fold a corner on your favorite page so you can find it again.
